newsitem.title: UGANDA: Hard-hit Uganda fights back at AIDS.
newsitem.headline: Hard-hit Uganda fights back at AIDS.

text.p: Uganda marked World AIDS Day on Sunday by saying it hoped to have turned the tide on a disease which has struck 10 percent of its population and cut average life expectancy by 10 years.
Ugandan AIDS Control Manager Dr Elizabeth Madraa noted latest official figures showed the incidence of HIV infection, which can lead on to AIDS, had fallen in some urban areas.
"The incidence of AIDS has dropped dramatically in the 14 to 24 year-old age group -- a clear result of the campaign to increase awareness of the danger AIDS represents," she said.

Health ministry figures show 1.8 million people -- 10 percent of Uganda's population -- have the HIV virus and that more than 46,000 people are known to suffer from full blown AIDS. But officials admit the AIDS figure could be three times higher because of the limited range of health services.
As the first African country to confront the disease, Uganda is also among the few states in the world's poorest continent with an effective AIDS surveillance system, medical experts say.

The anti-AIDS campaign places special emphasis through countrywide publicity on schools and youth groups, as well as vulnerable groups such as truck drivers. In the last three years this policy has produced encouraging results.

"We did a validation. When we compared the results from ante-natal clinics, where we do our surveillance for monitoring, we have identified in the last three years a decline in those centres where we were formerly seeing a very, very high peak.
"Something is happening. Of course, that's not a true representation of the entire population, but it shows that something is being done," said Dr Madraa.

This is good news in a country where health services are severely overstretched, with only one doctor for every 50,000 or AIDS workers in Uganda say it has fought the virus more openly and aggressively than any other African country. It was the first in Africa to target AIDS as a priority area, with help from western donors.

"This year there's no donor funding, but the government is ready to fund the entire AIDS programme for this year," said Dr Madraa. "And the government has gone further to borrow money from the World Bank for (dealing with) our work on sexually transmitted infections."
The major thrust of the campaign is to create the widest possible awareness of AIDS.

"In the urban centres, more and more people now know the value of condoms as a preventative measure," Dr Madraa told Reuters. "The political commitment has given an openness about the matter, which we've been using for HIV-AIDS control and prevention."
Poverty and communication problems, however, mean that Uganda's rural areas, where the majority of the population live, are slower to respond to the AIDS campaign.
The first AIDS case in Uganda was reported in 1982 in the southern district of Rakai -- still one of the worst-affected areas. One in four families there have an AIDS-related problem.

Across Uganda the damage caused by AIDS has been dramatic. Figures from the World Health Organisation (WHO) reveal that between 1980 and 1994 average life expectancy dropped from 52 to 42, among the lowest in the world.
By the year 2010, life expectancy could fall to 31 -- unless the limited successes now being reported in the anti-AIDS campaign can be sustained and expanded.
